all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: augmented reality
concepts.definition: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.

defining_facts.text: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
Augmented reality (AR), unlike virtual reality (VR), does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content.
Augmented reality (AR) applications include archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, commerce (particularly e-commerce), gaming, and medical domains, among other domains.
In archaeology, augmented reality (AR) can display things that are not visible to the naked eye on a screen and can reconstruct lost structures.
In industrial manufacturing, augmented reality (AR) can allow a person to see things while repairing or troubleshooting a component of an industrial setup.
The presence of many augmented reality (AR) applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.
Pokemon Go is a famous augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

Augmented reality (AR) is defined by the Merriam-Webster dictionary as an enhanced version of reality created by the use of technology, primarily computer technology, to overlay digital information on an image of something being viewed through a device.

The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.
An augmented reality (AR) system can superimpose extra information, such as non-existent furniture, as digital content over the real-world view of a room.

The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.

Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: display
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a display or output device is used in a broad sense to mean any device that produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs, not only a visual display.
A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.
The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.

A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.

The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

concepts.name: rotation
concepts.definition: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

defining_facts.text: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

concepts.name: rendering
concepts.definition: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.

defining_facts.text: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.
In the context of creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the terms view or rendering are used in a broad sense to refer not only to visual output but also to output for other senses.

From the developer's point of view, virtual reality (VR) software should allow the developer to create a VR application by providing assistance in the three activities of creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.

Rendering, the key component of any immersive experience in which the scene is rendered in front of the user's eyes on the display device, is covered by computer graphics, so some knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved in rendering.

concepts.name: three-dimensional graphics pipeline
concepts.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.

defining_facts.text: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.
The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.
The first stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, object representation, defines the objects that together form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system.

The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.

The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, scan conversion, transforms the continuous device coordinate system description, whose points can take real-number coordinates, into the discrete pixel-grid or screen coordinate system, where each pixel coordinate is an integer.

Transforming an object definition to a pixel-level scene description in the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline uses six coordinate systems: the local coordinate system, the world coordinate system, the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, the device coordinate system, and the pixel-grid or screen coordinate system.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline consists of five stages in order: object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling transformation, which transforms a local coordinate description to a world coordinate description; lighting, which takes place in the world coordinate reference frame; the viewing pipeline, which contains viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to a three-dimensional view coordinate system, clipping in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; and scan conversion, which transforms the device coordinate scene description to a screen coordinate or pixel grid description.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline has five stages, and the first four stages are object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling or geometric transformation from the local coordinate system to the world coordinate system; lighting in the world coordinate system; and viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

In the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, after the viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the scan conversion stage, also called the rendering stage, which transforms a device coordinate description into a screen coordinate description on the pixel grid.

concepts.name: clipping
concepts.definition: Scene graph-based representations support operations that are part of a three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, including sorting objects according to visibility (visible surface detection), removing objects outside the camera field of view (clipping), state management, and higher-level abstractions of functionality.

defining_facts.text: Scene graph-based representations support operations that are part of a three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, including sorting objects according to visibility (visible surface detection), removing objects outside the camera field of view (clipping), state management, and higher-level abstractions of functionality.
Clipping is the process of discarding objects that are part of the scene but outside the view volume, and it takes place before projection.

To project a point P from the world coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view plane, P is first transformed to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, then the view volume containing P is transformed to a canonical view volume before clipping, and finally the point in the canonical view volume is projected onto the view plane; the final point P' is obtained by multiplying P by the world coordinate system to three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system transformation matrix, the canonical view volume transformation matrix, and the projection transformation matrix.

Clipping defines a view volume, discards objects or portions of objects outside that view volume, and is performed before projection so that projection is applied to fewer vertices and computational complexity is reduced.

concepts.name: graphics pipeline
concepts.definition: The graphics pipeline is the set of the distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.

defining_facts.text: The graphics pipeline is the set of the distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.

concepts.name: world coordinate system
concepts.definition: The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.

defining_facts.text: The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.

The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

The world coordinate system is the reference frame in which all scene points are defined.

The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point.

The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is view transformation, which is also called the viewing pipeline.

The basic idea of view transformation, which is the viewing pipeline, is that an image on a screen or head-mounted display (HMD) is produced by selecting a portion of a three-dimensional (3D) scene and projecting the portion onto a two-dimensional (2D) display or view plane.

The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.
The sequence of stages or sub-stages in the viewing pipeline is not fixed, because different implementations can alter the sequence.

The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy).

In the window-to-viewport transformation, the transformation matrix is a three by three matrix whose Sx is defined in terms of the viewport and window dimensions along the x-axis, whose Sy is similarly defined with respect to the viewport and window dimensions along the y-axis, and whose Tx and Ty are computed in terms of Sx and Sy and the corresponding x-axis or y-axis window and viewport dimensions.

To obtain the transformed viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by the window-to-viewport transformation matrix, and because the resulting point is in homogeneous coordinate representation, the Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the result by the homogeneous factor W.

Rendering is the most challenging part of immersive experience generation from the point of view of the system.

The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the scan conversion stage, also called the rendering stage, which transforms a device coordinate description into a screen coordinate description on the pixel grid.

Scan conversion, also called rendering or rasterization, is, after the earlier four stages, the fifth stage in which mapping algorithms transform continuous two-dimensional (2D) viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a line is rendered by coloring specific pixels.

concepts.name: translation
concepts.definition: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.

defining_facts.text: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.

In the worked example, transforming rectangle ABCD from its local coordinate system to the chimney-like shape A′, B′, C′, D′ in the world coordinate scene cannot be done with one basic transformation and requires two basic transformations, scaling and translation.

In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and the transformed chimney shape A′, B′, C′, D′, the scaling matrix has Sx (the scaling factor along the x direction) equal to 0.5 and Sy (the scaling factor along the y direction) equal to 1 because the object is halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and the translation matrix has Tx (translation along the x-axis) equal to 5 and Ty (translation along the y-axis) equal to 5 because vertex D at (0, 0) moves to D′ at (5, 5).

In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and A′, B′, C′, D′, scaling is applied first and translation is applied second, so the translation matrix is placed to the left of the scaling matrix and the two matrices are multiplied to obtain the composite transformation matrix.

concepts.name: scaling
concepts.definition: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

defining_facts.text: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

concepts.definition: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

concepts.name: composite transformation matrix
concepts.definition: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.

defining_facts.text: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.

A composite transformation matrix is formed by arranging the individual transformation matrices from right to left according to the order of application: the first transformation applied is placed rightmost, each subsequent transformation is placed to its left, and the matrices are multiplied.

In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and A′, B′, C′, D′, scaling is applied first and translation is applied second, so the translation matrix is placed to the left of the scaling matrix and the two matrices are multiplied to obtain the composite transformation matrix.

To obtain transformed vertices in the world coordinate scene, each current vertex is multiplied by the transformation matrix; in the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and A′, B′, C′, D′, A′ = M A, B′ = M B, C′ = M C, and D′ = M D, where M is the composite transformation matrix.

Once the view coordinate system is defined, the three-dimensional (3D) transformation from world coordinates to view coordinates is performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix that is the product of the rotation and translation transformation matrices; a point in view coordinates is obtained by multiplying the corresponding world-coordinate point vector by this matrix, and the matrices are formed from the view-coordinate axis vectors and their scalar components.

never_defined.name: reference frame
never_defined.definition: Location-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications rely on a location sensor, such as a global positioning system (GPS) sensor, to detect the user's location with respect to a reference frame, and digital content is augmented on the real-world view when the user is at a specific location.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional scene
never_defined.definition: The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

never_defined.name: projector
never_defined.definition: The Microsoft HoloLens includes two depth cameras, one noise-cancelling microphone, a speaker, a port for attaching headphones, special glasses that project digital content onto the regular real-world view, a tilt mechanism, nose pads, one camera, one projector, sensors, a high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) optical head-mounted display (HMD), and spatial audio capabilities.

never_defined.name: point
never_defined.definition: In natural feature tracking, the advanced image processing algorithms or computer vision techniques detect features that are unique to the surroundings with respect to the object to be tracked, such as points, corners, and line intersections.

never_defined.name: surface
never_defined.definition: Physics support in a virtual world generator should also replicate other physical-world phenomena, such as how light propagates, how light interacts with different surfaces, the effects generated, the sources of light and resulting illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate.

never_defined.name: projection
never_defined.definition: In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect.

never_defined.name: object
never_defined.definition: When a hand touches an object, activated somatosensory receptors transform the input into neural impulses that are transmitted through a neural network from neuron to neuron to the brain, and the brain processes these impulses into touch perception and can send messages back through the same pathway to cause corrective motor actions, such as removing the hand from a hot object, and the same process is equally applicable to the proprioceptive sense.

never_defined.name: vertex
never_defined.definition: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional view coordinate system
never_defined.definition: Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

never_defined.name: matrix
never_defined.definition: Each transformation is typically represented by a matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system, where one extra dimension is added, so a two-dimensional (2D) transformation can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix and a three-dimensional (3D) transformation can be represented by a 4 by 4 matrix.

never_defined.name: transformation matrix
never_defined.definition: A point (x, y) in an object's local coordinate system can be transformed to the world coordinate system by representing the point as the column vector P, multiplying it by the transformation matrix S to obtain the new point P dash, and thereby performing a matrix multiplication of points on the object's surface into new points that ideally should be in the world coordinate system.

never_defined.name: surface point
never_defined.definition: A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived.

never_defined.name: vector
never_defined.definition: In a colored light source model, emitted light intensity has three components corresponding to the primary colors red, green, and blue, rather than a single component, and the source intensity is the three-element vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).

never_defined.name: two-dimensional display
never_defined.definition: The basic idea of view transformation, which is the viewing pipeline, is that an image on a screen or head-mounted display (HMD) is produced by selecting a portion of a three-dimensional (3D) scene and projecting the portion onto a two-dimensional (2D) display or view plane.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional world coordinate system
never_defined.definition: The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

never_defined.name: two-dimensional view plane
never_defined.definition: The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

never_defined.name: two-dimensional device coordinate space
never_defined.definition: The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

never_defined.name: world coordinates
never_defined.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters.

never_defined.name: view coordinates
never_defined.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters.

never_defined.name: camera viewing mechanism
never_defined.definition: The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters.

never_defined.name: view-up point
never_defined.definition: The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point.

never_defined.name: center of interest
never_defined.definition: The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point.

never_defined.name: looking direction
never_defined.definition: The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

never_defined.name: view-up direction
never_defined.definition: The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

never_defined.name: origin point
never_defined.definition: The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

never_defined.name: cross product
never_defined.definition: The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

never_defined.name: view-coordinate axis vector
never_defined.definition: Once the view coordinate system is defined, the three-dimensional (3D) transformation from world coordinates to view coordinates is performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix that is the product of the rotation and translation transformation matrices; a point in view coordinates is obtained by multiplying the corresponding world-coordinate point vector by this matrix, and the matrices are formed from the view-coordinate axis vectors and their scalar components.

never_defined.definition: Once the view coordinate system is defined, the three-dimensional (3D) transformation from world coordinates to view coordinates is performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix that is the product of the rotation and translation transformation matrices; a point in view coordinates is obtained by multiplying the corresponding world-coordinate point vector by this matrix, and the matrices are formed from the view-coordinate axis vectors and their scalar components.

never_defined.name: frustum
never_defined.definition: For parallel projection, the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped-shaped region, and for perspective projection, the view volume is a frustum, with one face or side of the view volume serving as the clipping window on which objects inside the view volume are projected.

never_defined.name: unit cube
never_defined.definition: A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube into which any arbitrarily defined view volume for parallel or perspective projection is converted in order to simplify pipeline computations.

never_defined.name: point vector
never_defined.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

never_defined.name: origin
never_defined.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

never_defined.name: homogeneous coordinate value
never_defined.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

never_defined.name: homogeneous factor
never_defined.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

never_defined.name: cartesian coordinate
never_defined.definition: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

never_defined.name: device space
never_defined.definition: A viewport is not defined on the view plane but in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, and it is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and the screen or display dimensions.

never_defined.name: window point
never_defined.definition: The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy).

never_defined.name: viewport point
never_defined.definition: The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy).

never_defined.name: homogeneous coordinate representation
never_defined.definition: To obtain the transformed viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by the window-to-viewport transformation matrix, and because the resulting point is in homogeneous coordinate representation, the Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the result by the homogeneous factor W.

never_defined.name: cartesian point
never_defined.definition: To obtain the transformed viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by the window-to-viewport transformation matrix, and because the resulting point is in homogeneous coordinate representation, the Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the result by the homogeneous factor W.

never_defined.name: computational complexity
never_defined.definition: Clipping defines a view volume, discards objects or portions of objects outside that view volume, and is performed before projection so that projection is applied to fewer vertices and computational complexity is reduced.

never_defined.name: viewer position
never_defined.definition: Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

never_defined.name: occlusion
never_defined.definition: Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.
